newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan vehicle output marks biggest gain since 1980.
newsitem.headline: Japan vehicle output marks biggest gain since 1980.

text.p: Japan's monthly vehicle production marked its biggest year-on-year gain since 1980 in January, helped by strong domestic demand ahead of a sales-tax increase, and higher exports due to a weaker yen.
Domestic production rose more than 19 percent compared with January last year to 917,798 vehicles, the Japan Automobile Manufacturers' Association (JAMA) said on Monday.
It was the fifth successive month of year-on-year gains and the biggest since a nearly 24 percent gain in September 1980, a JAMA official said.

JAMA said it expects exports in January to show a sharp 34 percent rise from a year earlier and added that this was likely to provoke complaints from the U.S. car industry about the growth in exports.
"The American car industry may complain about higher January exports but the higher exports were mainly because Japan had lower exports in January last year," a JAMA official said.

Tokyo's Finance Ministry said last week that Japan's trade surplus with the United States soared by more than 80 percent in January from a year earlier to 298.34 billion yen ($2.44 billion), mainly due to higher exports of cars and personal computers.

JAMA said the output increase was a result of strong domestic demand in the first quarter of 1997 ahead of a scheduled increase in Japan's consumption tax from three to five percent on April 1, and higher exports due to the weaker yen.
The yen traded at about 106 yen to the dollar in January 1996 compared with about 123 yen at the end of this January.
JAMA said production rose at all 11 Japanese vehicle makers rose this January and domestic sales, including those of 660 cc mini vehicles, rose 11.5 percent from a year earlier to 446,192.
A JAMA official said production and exports in February are likely to be down from February last year because of lost production at Toyota Motor Corp caused by a February 1 fire at a parts-supplier.
Toyota said on February 17 that lost production from the fire would total about 70,000 vehicles.
A spokesman for the firm said it would not be able to make up the loss by March but hoped to by April.
